\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Benchmark scores drive model selection, resource allocation, and research priorities for large language models, yet training data contamination undermines the validity of these scores in ways that current evaluation cannot quantify \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,chang2025benchmarking}. When models encounter test items during training, observed accuracy conflates genuine capability with memorization, and practitioners have no principled way to determine how much of a reported score reflects real understanding. The problem is compounded by the scale of modern training corpora: trillion-token web crawls make contamination pervasive and instance-level measurement infeasible \citep{oren2024proving}. Post-hoc calibration that quantifies contamination effects despite imperfect detection is therefore essential for trustworthy evaluation.

Two developments make this gap urgent. First, \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty contamination mitigation strategies (rephrasing, option shuffling, dynamic benchmark regeneration, and others) and demonstrate that none restores clean performance after contamination has occurred. This result forecloses the ``prevent contamination'' approach for models already trained on unrestricted web data. Second, contamination-free benchmarks \citep{white2024livebench} offer a partial solution but sacrifice the comparability and institutional knowledge accumulated around established benchmarks. Dynamic regeneration of test items may also be contaminated within weeks as web crawlers index benchmark repositories \citep{dong_2024_cdd}. The field therefore needs post-hoc statistical tools that can separate genuine ability from contamination artifacts on existing benchmarks.

Detection methods such as Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang_2024_minkpp}, ConStat \citep{dekoninck2024constat}, and Kernel Divergence Signatures \citep{choi_2025_kds} can flag contaminated items but stop at detection. They do not quantify how much scores are inflated or produce adjusted scores with uncertainty estimates. Score adjustment methods like DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} provide point corrections without uncertainty quantification or a principled measurement framework. IRT-based evaluation frameworks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks,habba_2025_growing_pains} apply psychometric ability estimation to improve evaluation efficiency, but they treat all items as equally trustworthy and ignore contamination entirely \citep{lalor_2024_irt_nlp}. These two research threads have developed in isolation: detection papers end at binary flags, while IRT papers assume clean data. No existing method bridges detection signals and a measurement-theoretic calibration framework to produce decontaminated ability estimates with credible intervals.

This paper asks: does calibrating contaminated scores require accurate per-item detection, or can a principled measurement model separate ability from noise more generally? We develop ContamCal to investigate this question. Stage~1 fuses multiple detection signals into continuous per-item exposure scores via training-free Reciprocal Rank Fusion \citep{cormack_2009_rrf}, avoiding the meta-circularity of learned aggregators that would require the very contamination labels we lack. Stage~2 embeds these exposure scores as covariates in a contamination-augmented IRT model (2PL+$\gamma$) that jointly estimates latent ability $\theta$ and a domain-level contamination effect $\gamma_k$. Our experiments yield a clear empirical finding: IRT ability estimation itself accounts for the dominant calibration benefit. Vanilla 2PL without any contamination parameter reduces calibration error on ARC by 53\% (MAE from 0.034 to 0.016), comparable to the full 2PL+$\gamma$ model. The calibration comes from IRT's measurement structure, which separates stable capability from item-level noise regardless of contamination modeling. Preliminary cross-family evidence from Llama-3.2-3B ($N=3$--$4$, single seed) suggests this benefit extends across architectures. The $\gamma$ parameter serves a complementary diagnostic role within a family, revealing the direction of contamination effects across cognitive domains.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Empirical calibration decomposition.} We find that IRT ability estimation provides calibration benefit independent of whether contamination is explicitly modeled through $\gamma$: vanilla 2PL reduces MAE by up to 53\% on the primary Qwen2.5 ensemble ($J=13$). Preliminary cross-family evidence from Llama-3.2-3B ($N=3$--$4$, single seed) suggests calibrated MAE remains below 0.02 when pooling across architectures.
    \item \textbf{Exposure-based item selection via RRF.} We develop a training-free signal fusion pipeline that enables targeted item selection for calibration: on full MMLU (14k items, ${\sim}2\%$ contaminated), IRT without selection yields $\tau = 0.024$; with RRF-based selection, $\tau = 0.637$. S1 dominates in practice; S2 and S4 are actively harmful at 0.5B (\S\ref{sec:signal_failure}).
    \item \textbf{Detection signal failure modes.} We document a directional reversal in Min-K\%++ at model scales below 1.5B parameters (Cohen's $d = -1.55$ to $-1.98$), where the signal is actively misleading rather than merely ineffective. This finding has immediate practical consequences for contamination detection at small scales.
    \item \textbf{Identifiability boundaries for $\gamma$ recovery.} Simulation studies establish that reliable $\gamma$ recovery requires signal AUC $\geq 0.55$ and $J \geq 50$, a threshold well above current LLM evaluation practice ($J = 8$--$30$). This result delineates when contamination-augmented IRT transitions from exploratory to confirmatory.
    \item \textbf{Exploratory domain-level diagnosis.} Within-family analysis at $J = 13$ reveals directional heterogeneity across MMLU cognitive domains, with Social Sciences ($\gamma = -0.57$) reaching significance in independent per-domain fitting without multiple comparison correction. Domain-level $\gamma$ patterns are family-specific and do not generalize across architectures.
\end{enumerate}

Current approaches include Min-K\% \citep{shi_2023_minkprob} and Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang_2024_minkpp} (token-level surprisal), ConStat \citep{dekoninck2024constat} (accuracy gaps on paraphrased items), CDD/TED \citep{dong_2024_cdd} (completion-based probes), KDS \citep{choi_2025_kds} (kernel divergence), TS-Guessing \citep{deng_2024_tsguessing} (temporal splits), and Time Travel \citep{golchin_2024_time_travel} (guided generation probes). Concurrent with our work, \citet{tao2025detecting} propose an entropy collapse method for RL-trained models. \citet{kocyigit2025impact} show that post-training procedures (RLHF, DPO) degrade detection signal reliability, complicating the application of token-level methods to instruction-tuned models. \citet{zhang_2024_gsm1k} construct GSM1K as a parallel test set to quantify GSM8K contamination, demonstrating that performance gaps between original and regenerated items serve as a natural experiment for contamination measurement. These methods flag contamination but do not produce adjusted scores. On the mitigation side, \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty approaches and find that none reliably restores clean performance; inference-time decontamination \citep{yang2024inference} and decontamination via forgetting \citep{zhang2025forget} similarly show limited effectiveness. DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} estimates decontaminated scores via fuzzy inference but produces point estimates without uncertainty quantification or domain-level diagnosis. ContamCal consumes detection signals as inputs and feeds them into a calibration framework that estimates decontaminated ability with credible intervals.
\paragraph{IRT for LLM evaluation.}

-Item Response Theory has gained traction as a principled alternative to raw accuracy. \citet{lalor_2024_irt_nlp} provide a comprehensive IRT tutorial for NLP; TinyBenchmarks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks} uses IRT-informed item selection for efficient evaluation; Growing Pains \citep{habba_2025_growing_pains} validates IRT at scale on 400+ models and identifies low-respondent limitations; HiBayES \citep{luettgau_2025_hibayes} adds hierarchical Bayesian inference for credible intervals; ATLAS \citep{li_2024_atlas} applies IRT for adaptive testing. Most directly related, PSN-IRT \citep{zhou_2025_psnirt} applies IRT to LLM benchmarks with prompt sensitivity as a difficulty axis, but does not model contamination effects and assumes all items are trustworthy. ContamCal differs by introducing contamination covariates $\gamma_k$ that explicitly capture how exposure shifts item difficulty, enabling both calibration and per-domain contamination diagnosis.

\paragraph{Differential item functioning and explanatory IRT.}

ContamCal's $\gamma$ parameter is formally an instance of explanatory DIF \citep{holland_1993_dif,thissen1993dif}: it models how an item-level covariate (contamination exposure) differentially affects response probability across items. In educational measurement, DIF detects unfairness when items function differently across demographic groups \citep{zumbo1999dif}; in our setting, the ``group'' variable is contamination status and the DIF direction indicates whether exposure inflates or deflates performance. We build on the explanatory IRT tradition \citep{deboeck_2004_explanatory_irt}, which incorporates item and person covariates directly into the response model rather than treating them as post-hoc diagnostics. The item compromise literature \citep{eckerly_2017_item_compromise,sinharay_2017_preknowledge} provides the closest psychometric precedent, modeling preknowledge effects on compromised items. Our adaptations for LLM evaluation are: continuous (not binary) exposure scores, domain-level stratification, and counterfactual inference via posterior expectation under zero exposure (\S\ref{sec:formulation}).
